etymologies.etymologyHTML: From late Middle English noughti, naughty (“evil, immoral, wicked”), from nought (“evil, immoral”) + -ī̆ (suffix forming adjectives). Analysable as naught +‎ -y.

definitions.definition: Mischievous; tending to misbehave or act badly (especially of a child). [from 17th c.]
Sexually provocative; now in weakened sense, risqué, cheeky. [from 19th c.]
(now rare, archaic) Evil, wicked, morally reprehensible. [from 15th c.]

quote.citation: 1589, John Bucke, Instructions for the Use of the Beades:
quote.text: my proneſſe to ſinne, and naughty appetites and desires, woulde drawe me headlong to the pitte of hell

quote.citation: c. 1596–1598 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Merchant of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene i]:
quote.text: […] How far that little candle throws his beams!So shines a good deed in a naughty world.

quote.citation: 1644, John Milton, Areopagitica; a Speech of Mr. John Milton for the Liberty of Unlicenc’d Printing, to the Parlament of England, London: [s.n.], →OCLC:
quote.text: Wholesome meats to a vitiated stomack differ little or nothing from unwholesome; and best books to a naughty mind are not unappliable to occasions of evill.

quote.citation: 1542, Andrew Boorde, The First Boke of the Introduction of Knowledge:
quote.text: In Cornwall is two speches, the one is naughty Englysshe, and the other is Cornysshe speche.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Jeremiah 24:2:
quote.text: One basket had very good figs, even like the figs that are first ripe: and the other basket had very naughty figs, which could not be eaten, they were so bad.
